newsitem.title: USA: Reverses in U.S. trade gains with Japan seen likely.
newsitem.headline: Reverses in U.S. trade gains with Japan seen likely.

text.p: Japan's effort to talk up the value of its currency comes at a time of growing worry among U.S. businesses that the dollar's strength against the yen will reverse hard won gains in reducing trade deficits.

After declining for several months, the huge U.S. trade deficit with Japan rose late last year. Some analysts saw that development, along with an announcement by Honda Motor Co. Ltd. that it would shift some U.S. production back to Japan, as a sign that the continuing strength of the dollar against the yen was starting to take a toll on trade.
"In my opinion the trade deficit with Japan has bottomed out, it has already started moving up," said Lawrence Chimerine, chief economist at the Economic Strategy Institute.
"Their own trade numbers for November clearly show their surplus with the U.S. is now starting to rise again. I think in the months ahead you will see that in our data," he said.
It could take as much as a year or more before the U.S. economy feels the full impact of the dollar's strength on the trade balance, analysts said.

A cheaper yen makes Japanese products more competitive in overseas markets, just as a stronger dollar makes U.S. goods less attractive. Some analysts said the impact of a weak yen may be far wider than the ability of a company to sell a product or not.

"What we really want is for Japan to restructure its economy," Norwest Corp. chief economist Sung Won Sohn said. "They have too many regulations and they need to reduce them and allow more imports. For a while when dollar was weak and yen strong, they were under pressure to reform their economy. Right now things look pretty nice and hunky-dory so they don't have any incentive to change."

When the dollar dropped as low as 80 yen in early 1995, Japanese manufacturers had a powerful incentive to break cosy business relationships -- which frustrate U.S. firms trying to get into Japanese markets -- and seek foreign suppliers, one U.S. official suggested. A strong dollar and weak yen removes that incentive.
The dollar rose to a 46-month high of 117 yen on Monday, prompting comments by Japanese officials that they were concerned about excessive movements in the currency.
"An excessively weak or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy," Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a press conference on Tuesday. "We want exchange rates to stabilise."
U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin has often voiced support for a strong dollar, which helps keeps prices and interest rates low in the United States.

American Automobile Manufacturers Association president Andrew Card suggested the Japanese government may be feeling some heat from Japanese companies who have moved production to other countries and are being hurt by the weak yen.
U.S. car makers have complained that the weak yen hurts efforts to break into the Japanese car and parts markets.
"The pressure to bring meaningful reform to the Japanese economy is diminished with an excessively weak yen," Card said.

U.S. parts manufacturers are likely to feel the impact hardest, despite a 1995 trade agreement between the United States and Japan aimed at opening Japan's car and parts markets and encouraging more U.S. original parts sales to Japanese car manufacturers. The strong dollar makes their products more costly to Japanese manufacturers, Card said.
